title: Eco-tariff

definition.text: An eco-tariff, or environmental tariff, is a trade barrier such as an import or export tax used to reduce pollution.

facts.text: It targets goods with a large carbon footprint or goods from countries with lax environmental rules; a carbon tariff is one type.
Supporters say it could stop foreign countries gaining advantage from weak rules and bring trading partners' standards into line.
Critics argue it reduces trade without reaching the main sources of pollution, much of which arises within a country's own borders.
Developing countries fear it as green protectionism: using environmental goals as cover for shielding domestic industry.
Tariffs on imports alone can weaken export competitiveness and contribute to deindustrialisation.

contested_note: There is debate over whether freer international trade increases pollution or, by raising incomes, ends up reducing it.

definition.text: Effluent is wastewater from sewers or industrial outlets that flows into rivers, lakes or the sea, either treated or untreated.

facts.text: It can carry fats and oils, solvents, detergents, heavy metals and food waste from many industries.
Warm cooling-water effluent from power stations causes thermal pollution.
In the US the Clean Water Act requires a permit for every direct discharge of effluent into surface waters.

definition.text: An excise is a tax on a particular category of goods, usually charged when they are made for sale at home.

facts.text: Unlike a sales tax or VAT charged as a share of the price, an excise is usually a fixed amount per unit, falls on few products and is heavier.
It is an indirect tax: the producer pays it but is expected to pass it on to buyers through higher prices.
Tobacco, alcohol and fuel are its three main targets in most countries.
Excises can correct externalities by charging for costs that buyers or sellers impose on society but that prices leave out.
Excises are increasingly placed on polluting transport and on products that create hard-to-recycle waste.

definition.text: A feebate charges a fee on products with harmful side effects and uses the money to give rebates on cleaner alternatives.

facts.text: Feebates are usually revenue-neutral, with the fees paying for the rebates.
Arthur H. Rosenfeld coined the idea in the 1970s; it has mostly been used in transport and energy.
Car buyers discount future fuel costs heavily, so a feebate puts the cost into the purchase price where it is noticed.
